content:
What if your legal rights are clear, but someone refuses to recognize them?
You may not always need compensation or possession of property. 
Sometimes, what you need first is a courts formal recognition of your rights.
This is where a suit for declaration becomes relevant.
A common misconception is that every legal dispute requires the court to order someone to do something. 
Under Section 34 of Indias Specific Relief Act, 1963, a person may seek a declaration that they are legally entitled to a particular status or right, such as ownership of property or a legal status being disputed.
Heres the crucial distinction: a declaration is not always the only remedy available, and it cannot replace every other form of relief. 
If you could seek further relief, such as possession of property, but deliberately omit that claim, the court generally cannot grant a bare declaration under Section 34. For example, if someone disputes your ownership while you remain in possession, a declaration may address the disputed right. 
But if you have been unlawfully dispossessed, you may also need to seek possession.
The practical takeaway?
 Identify exactly what right is being denied and whether recognition alone will resolve the dispute.
 The relief you choose can determine the effectiveness of your case. In your view, when should a person seek a declaration alone, and when should they combine it with another remedy?
 The distinction can make a significant difference in litigation.

Adv. Smriti Kumari (Tiwari)
Advocate | Patna High Court, Bihar
